title: Neural Synchrony Between Socially Interacting Language Models
claim: We measure social alignment by extracting hidden states from interacting agents and fitting predictive mappings between them over time.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right then top-to-bottom, colored section banners, timeline with arrows
description: A three-stage figure with light-blue banner headers: Agent Social Interaction, Representation Extraction, and Neural Synchrony Measurement. The left panel shows two persona cards. Gwen is an extraverted architect and Oliver is a conscientious social worker, each with a goal about buying or selling a TV. Under the cards, a chat shows a price negotiation, with speech bubbles alternating between the two avatars at t=0, 1 and 2. The top-right panel shows each avatar's hidden representation passing through frozen LLM blocks, one green and one yellow, with the layers labelled h_l and h_{l+1}. Curved arrows link the utterances to the extracted representations. The bottom-right panel shows a timeline of representations h^A and h^B at successive turns, joined by blue arrows labelled as predictive affine transformations. A note lists what these capture: social engagement and temporal dynamics.
caption: An illustration of our analysis framework. (1) Two LLM agents engage in a social interaction, generating responses conditioned on their backgrounds, goals, and shared history. (2) Hidden representations are extracted at each turn from both LLMs. (3) Neural synchrony is measured by learning affine mappings to predict one agent’s future representations from the other’s current ones.
abstract: Neuroscience has uncovered a fundamental mechanism of our social nature: human brain activity becomes synchronized with others in many social contexts involving interaction. Traditionally, social minds have been regarded as an exclusive property of living beings. Although large language models (LLMs) are widely accepted as powerful approximations of human behavior, with multi-LLM system being extensively explored to enhance their capabilities, it remains controversial whether they can be meaningfully compared to human social minds. In this work, we explore neural synchrony between socially interacting LLMs as an empirical evidence for this debate. Specifically, we introduce neural synchrony during social simulations as a novel proxy for analyzing the sociality of LLMs at the representational level. Through carefully designed experiments, we demonstrate that it reliably reflects both social engagement and temporal alignment in their interactions. Our findings indicate that neural synchrony between LLMs is strongly correlated with their social performance, highlighting an important link between neural synchrony and the social behaviors of LLMs. Our work offers a new perspective to examine the "social minds" of LLMs, highlighting surprising parallels in the internal dynamics that underlie human and LLM social interaction.
